title: The Efficiency Trap
coreMove: Use efficiency only after choosing your losses; saved minutes become new demands unless a finite person names what will not get done, desired, or improved.

exampleSpecs.audience: program coordinators tempted to pack a schedule
exampleSpecs.stakes: A playful morning can become overload if every good activity gets squeezed in.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Use Busytown's cheerful fullness to show why a real schedule needs loss.

exampleSpecs.stakes: A better tool may quietly raise the promise residents expect.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Show labor-saving equipment resetting standards upward.

exampleSpecs.audience: high achievers whose status depends on constant output
exampleSpecs.stakes: The reward for winning can become a larger claim on time.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Show meritocratic success increasing pressure rather than relieving it.

exampleSpecs.audience: families tempted to erase every inconvenience
exampleSpecs.stakes: Removing friction may remove the chosen life that friction served.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Show Keesmaat's inconvenient routine as a chosen value, not a defect.

exampleSpecs.audience: support leads who reward fast processing
exampleSpecs.stakes: A clean queue can teach others to route more work to the same person.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Show fast processing attracting added demand.

exampleSpecs.audience: readers who fill saved time with new options
exampleSpecs.stakes: New capacity can expand appetite instead of creating rest.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Show saved time revealing more possibilities than a finite person can live.
